speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
This Bill is purely technical in its character. Where patents have been issued for lands situated within a

forest reserve and where an incorrect description has been given of the individual, his occupation, or even of the lands themselves, the Minister of the Interior is authorized to cancel the letters patent and issue letters patent with the necesary corrections or alterations. Under the Dominion Lands Act as at present he has that authority in respect of lands outside the forest reserves, but there is a doubt as to whether the Dominion Lands Act applies to lands within the forest reserves. This is intended to clear up that doubt and to confer upon the Minister of the Interior the same power within the reserves that he has without.

Consideration of the proposed motion oi Sir Wilfrid Laurier for a committee to inquire into purchases of shells or other munitions or goods by the Shell Committee, resumed from Tuesday, March 28.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before resuming my
argument at the point at which I moved the adjournment of the debate on Tuesday night last, I desire to refer to a previous portion of the speech of the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. G. W. Kyte) and to certain allegations made by him and by the hon. member for Carleton, N.B. (Mr. F. B. Carvell), respecting contracts let by the Shell Committee, in which it was argued that discrimination had been exercised for political considerations against the Dominion Iron and Steel Company. As I have stated, the Government is not in any way responsible for the contracts let by the Shell Committee. The Government of Canada has had no authority over the Shell Committee in the letting of its contracts; but the statements made by the hon. member for Richmond and by the hon. member for Carleton with respect to the matter with which I now purpose dealing appear to me to be so much beside the facts that I deem it my duty not to leave the record in its present condition.
The hon. member for Carleton, speaking on March 7, and alleging discrimination for political reasons against the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, called attention to the fact that the Shell Committee, while awarding large contracts to the Nova Scotia Steel Company, had passed over the Dominion Iron and Steel Company. His words were as follows:
The Dominion Iron and Steel Company, probably the greatest manufacturing establishment in the whole Dominion, who were anxious for the business, who were willing to devote their whole organization, machinery, plant and business facilities to the manufacture of shells, and who pleaded and begged in vain for an order.
He alleges that the fact that Mr. Frederick Nicholls was connected with the Dominion Iron and Steel Company had something to do with the fact that the Dominion Iron and Steel Company got no work from the Shell Committee. He says:
They never got a chance to do business, never got a look in until October or November, 1915.
The hon. member for Richmond, coming, as I have stated, to the rescue of the hon.

member for Carleton afteT his argument had been met by the hon. Solicitor General, used the following language:
The Dominion Iron and Steel Company is located in my new constituency which was bestowed upon me by the Government in the late distribution of seats.
He says further:
I knew that the Dominion Iron and Steel Company had no contracts for shells, and when I heard the Solicitor General speak with all the authority which such a statement should possess coming from him as a member of this Government, and with all the access he had to the sources of correct information, I was, to say the least astonished. I knew that for five or six months during 1915 the officials of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company travelled from Toronto to Ottawa, from Ottawa to Toronto, and from Toronto to Sydney, to get a contract to make shells, but they never got a contract for a single shell.
And then further on, at page 2368 of Hansard, he used the following language:
There is another circumstance in connection with that which perhaps hon. gentlemen do not realize, but which they will realize when I call their attention to it. Here was a contract given by the Shell Committee, not for shells, but for steel for shells. The Shell Committee bought that steel at Sydney, and instead of having it manufactured into shells there, as the Dominion Iron and Steel Company wanted them to do, they distributed it among shell factories all over Canada as far west as Vancouver, and paid freight on all these shipments; and then when the steel ingots were made into shells, the Shell Committee paid the freight on all these shells from Vancouver and the- other factories to the point of shipment.
My hon. friend was referring to the steel bought from the Dominion Iron and Steel Company by the Shell Committee, as he stated, on the 15th of May and the 2nd of April. I hold in my hand the report of the last annual meeting of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, which was held at Montreal on Thursday, the 24th day of June,. 1915; and I desire to call the attention of the House to the statement therein of the president of Dominion Iron and Steel Company, Mr. J. H. Plummer. He is speaking of the export business of the company, and this is his language:
Akin to this export 'business, and due to the same primary cause, is the business we are doing in the manufacture of shell steel. Many of you, no doubt, think we should long ago have been making shells, but that is out of our line. We can make excellent shell steel, and we have large orders for this, but its conversion into the finished shells is work for machine shops, of which there are plenty in the country.	-
What is the date of that?
OrdeT.
I know that the cackling of geese saved Rome from being destroyed, but the cadkling of geese -will not help this thing through.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is the report of the annual meeting, -held at Montreal on Thursday, the 24th day of June, 1915.
Exactly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
He said further:
We have, of course, good machine shops, but when we are running the plant fully, as we are now, they are barely sufficient for the maintenance and repair and replacement of the thousand and one mechanical parts which make up our very complex works. If we were to undertake the manufacture of shells-
He is speaking in June, 1915.

it would necessitate construction of entirely new shops, which would take a long time and much money. Of course, if it become necessary we must do our duty with the rest, but there are to my knowledge a great many shops now available, or in condition to be made available quickly, which have not yet received shell orders.
I call attention in this connection to the fact that the hon. member was speaking of the time the orders for shell steel were given to the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, on the 15th of May, 1915, when they got, he says, an order for 1,000,000 pieces of steel " to make shells out of," and, speaking also of the 2nd of April, 1915, when they got an order for 460,000 more pieces of steel "to make shells out of." He is speaking with regard to those transactions; yet the argument of my hon. friend is that they should have had orders not for steel for making shells, but for shells. He says:
The Shell Committee bought that steel at Sydney, and instead of having it manufactured into shells there, as the Dominion Iron and Steel Company wanted them to do.
Let me ask the House if, in the face of the statement of the President of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company on the 21th day of June, 1915, the hon. member for Richmond is within the facts in stating that the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, in April and May, wanted to manufacture shells.
I come now to the latter and the more important part of the speech of the hon. member for Richmond on Tuesday evening last. He referred, among other things, to contracts for the manufacture of fuses, two contracts entered into by the Shell Committee-with the American Ammunition Company in the one case and with the International Arms and Fuse Company in the other case. He stated that he would read from the contract with the American Ammunition Company because-and I do



not dissent from his statement-the two contracts were practically on all fours. Now, I desire to say again that as the Shell Committee was a committee acting as agents for the Imperial Government, the Government of Canada had not and could not have any responsibility for those two contracts so entered into by the Shell Committee. I have taken the trouble to obtain copies of the contracts, however, as the matter has been under discussion in this House, and there are certain features of them to which I desire to direct the attention of the House in order that there may be no misunderstanding as to the facts. The contract with the American Ammunition Company, which is substantially in the same form as the contract with the International Arms and Fuse Company, is dated the 19th day of June, 1915. It is made between the American Ammunition Company and the Shell Committee, a body appointed by the hon. the Minister of Militia and Defence of Canada.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: If that is so, that this Government had nothing at all to do with it, how is it that a Royal Commission has been issued to investigate it under Paragraph One of the Inquiries Act, which relates to investigations in respect to the good government of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will exercise patience, we shall come to that in due course. I am sorry to see that my hon. friend is losing that patience and urbanity which used to characterize him.
There is another feature of this contract to which I desire to draw the attention of the House, and, in that connection, I shall read the remarks of my hon. friend from Richmond on page 2374 of Hansard, in which he refers to the section of the agreement, in which power is given to the Shell Committee to cancel a contract in the event of default. My hon. friend had stated that' a large .advance payment of $1,000,000, or thereabouts, had been made, and after reading section 14 which gave, as I have stated, the right to the Shell Committee to cancel the contract in default of delivery, in accordance with its terms, my hon. friend from Richmond proceeded as follows:
That means that In default of delivery of the fuses they shall cancel parts of the contract and recover the amount back from the company. But how are they to do it? The company got one and one-half million dollars from the Shell Committee immediately on the execution of the contract and half a million more four months afterwards. Then, if the Shell Committee cancelled the contract, they lost the one and one-half-million dollars. Thus all they could do was to accept delivery when it suited the company to

make it, or they would lose all the money advanced to the company; and all they could do was to plead with the company to make deliveries.
I asked at the time he made that statement, or immediately laJterwards, if he had the guarantee which was referred to in the contract, and I understood him to state that he had not. For the information of the House only-because, as this matter is sub judice, I do not propose to discuss the merits of these contracts-and in order that the complete transaction may be before it, including the guarantee, I propose to read the form of guarantee which was given to the Shell Committee by .the Guaranty Trust Company of New York. The Guaranty Trust Company is' one of the most responsible financial institutions in New York. I think its total assets are in the neighbourhood of $350,000,000 or $360,000,000. I am informed by an hon. member beside me that $500,000,000 would be nearer the figure. However, there is no question as to the financial responsibility of the Guaranty Trust Company. I propose, as I stated, to read the . form of guarantee which was given by the Guaranty Trust Company in connection with this agreement, and in connection, also, with the agreement with the International Arms and Fuse Company. There is a guar-[DOT] antee covering the 10 per cent, which was to be at once advanced, and there are individual guarantees cowering the several other advances, which were to be made over a period of the first four months. The form of guarantee is as follows:
Guaranty Trust Company of New York hereby guarantee to the Shell Committee, of Ottawa, Canada, a body appointed by the hon. the Minister of Militia and Defence of Canada, the repayment to the said the Shell Committee by American Ammunition Company, Incorporated, of the city of New York, of the sum of one million and forty thousand ($1,040,000) dollars being an advance payment of ten per cent (10%) under the provisions of the agreement hereinafter mentioned, or such part or parts thereof from time to time, which, in the event of cancellation by said Shell Committee for non-deliveries, shall become repayable by said Ammunition Company to said the Shell Committee, under the provisions of paragraph 14 of an agreement in writing dated June 19th, 1915 between the American Ammunition Company, Incorporated, and said the Shell Committee for the purchase and sale of two and one half million (2,500,000) of fuses. The liability of this guarantee shall he reduced in amount from time to time as the' advance payments covered thereunder are applied in accordance with the terms of said contract of June 19th, 1915.
A guarantee, similar in form, covers the several payments aggregating 5 per cent
1571 '
of the amount of contract, which was to be made during the period of the first four months of the contract. Attached to the sevetral guarantees, to which I have referred, is an opinion by John F. Orde, Esq., K.C., of the city of Ottawa, of the firm of Orde, Powell & Lyle, addressed to the Shell Committee. It is in the following terms:
Re American Contract.
I have to-day examined the original guarantee dated the 8th day of July, 1915, of the Guaranty Trust Company, of New York, in the hands of the manager of the Bank of Montreal here, which guarantees to you the re-payment of the sum of $1,040,000 to be advanced by you in paragraph nine of the agreement with the American Ammunition Company of the 19tl>
of June, 1915, in the event of the company's making default thereunder. This guarantee has been executed under the corporate seal of the Guaranty Trust Company, of New York, and sufficiently guarantees to the Shell Committee the re-payment of the above-mentioned sum under the terms of the said agreement, and it is now in order for the committee to make the advance to the company of the above sum.
What is the date of that letter of Mr. J. F. Orde?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
July 13, 1915. I am placing these facts upon Hansard in order that the House may understand the nature of the contracts which were referred to by the hon. member for Richmond. In view of the fact that the hon. member read certain sections bearing on the matters to which he specially referred, I do not think it necessary that the entire contract should be placed upon Hansard. Apart from these contracts, my hon. friend did not place upon Hansard, and did not exhibit to the House, the other agreements with which he dealt. He referred to an agreement between Yoakum, Bassick, and E. B. Cadwell & Company, dealing with a commission of $1,000,000 for procuring a contract from the Shell Committee, and he Slated that tnat commission was at the rate of 40 cents per fuse, or about ten per cent of the contract. I have no knowledge whatever as to that contract, and as my hon. friend has not exhibited it to the House, and furthermore, as the matter is sub judice by reason of the determination of the Prime Minister to refer these transactions to a Royal Commission, I do not propose to deal with it any further, except to this extent.
After my hon. friend had recited the contract under which he alleges the parties in question agreed to divide a commission of $1,000,000 among themselves, he referred to

allegations, or suggestions, relating to any member of this Government in connection with contracts let by the Shell Committee of Canada.
Let us consider for a moment the personnel of this iCommission. The Commissioners chosen are two of the outstanding figures in the Canadian judiciary, Sir William Ralph Meredith, Chief Justice of Ontario, and Honourable Lyman P. Duff, one of the Justices of the Supreme Court of Canada. I do not believe that any member of this House, or any man in Canada, could take exception to these two eminent judges. I believe that these commissioners are acceptable to the people of Canada as men who will make a thorough, a fair, an unbiassed, an unprejudice judicial investigation into all the facts relating to these contracts and to any other that may be referred to them. Further than that, the leader of the Government has stated that as the Shell Committee is acting for "the Imperial Government, and as charges and allegations have been made in this House against the administration of the Shell Committee, he will direct the attention of the Imperial Government to every statement and assertion that may !be made in this House with respect to the conduct of the Shell Committee in carrying out its duty to the Imperial Government; and that if the Imperial Government desire an investigation into the expenditure of their money-for it is their money that has been expended-this Government will cooperate in any way possible, will create any commission, will appoint counsel, and will take all steps that may be necessary in order that such investigation may (be had at the instance of the Imperial Government. It seems to me that the Prime Minister has covered fully every contingency that can possibly arise in connection with the administration of the Shell Committee.
I was surprised, I confess, at the attitude of my right hon, friend the leader of the Opposition when the names of this commission were announced to the House. It is not often that the right hon. gentleman loses his poise, and it was to me a matter of supreme surprise that he should give away so manifestly to irritation at the announcement of these names. When the Prime Minister announced the personnel of the commission, the right hon. gentleman said:
Mr. Speaker, I regret to have to say to my right hon. friend and to the House that the proposal which he makes is absolutely unacfSir Thomas White.]	.
ceptable. If there is to be an inquiry, as he admits there bught to be an inquiry, that inquiry is to be made in this high court of Parliament.
Hear, (hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I hope my hon. friend will say " Hear, hear " a little later on-
When Parliament is sitting no other court is acceptable. Therefore I ask for the resumption of the discussion upon my motion.
Again the right hon. leader of the Opposition said:
There is a way, and that is to grant a committee. That is all I ask; nothing less and nothing more. I again ask to have the discussion on my motion resumed.
One might question why my right hon. friend decided that this investigation by a judicial commission, consisting of two of the most eminent, the most outstanding figures in the judicial life of Canada, was not acceptable to him. One would naturally ask: Does my right hon. friend desire to get at the very facts of the case-
All the facts.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, the facts, and all the facts of the case-or does he not?
We have had experience.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Personal experience, does the hon. gentleman mean? If the right hon. leader of the Opposition does desire to get at the facts-
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The right hon.
gentleman says "Hear, hear,"
4 p.m. and I repeat: If he desires to get at the facts,' what objection can he have to a commission empowered to inquire fully into all the facts?
Not all, by far.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Into all the facts -and a commission consisting, as I have said, of two men whose names will carry the confidence of every man in this country. My right hon. friend says that the proposal is entirely unacceptable.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The right hon. gentleman, from his attitude here to-day, and from his attitude when the personnel of the commission was announced, would have preferred to have a committee consisting of members of both sides of this House, a committee which, when constituted, would be divided on party lines, a committee

before which assertion, rumour, hearsay, insinuation, would be regarded as evidence; in which it would not be possible, as has been shown conclusively by the history of the past, that a fair, unprejudiced, unbiassed decision could be given, on an issue involving, as it does, the standing and reputation of a minister of the Crown. I assume that he would say that it would be fair that suggestions of this kind should be tried before a tribunal subject to delay from day to day and from week to week, and in which, as I have said, hearsay and innuendo would take the place of evidence. Or, is the truth more likely to be established before two judges of the eminence of the men who have been named, whose daily duty it is to sift evidence, to weigh evidence, to reach sound conclusions, and to mete out justice? Before which tribunal are we likely to establish the facts?
Mr. Speaker, in adopting the course which has been followed, and in appointing a commission for the purpose of thoroughly investigating these charges, the Government has been following sound precedent. All Governments have recognized that in questions of party controversy in which .partisan feeling runs high, adjudication should be by commission and not by committee.
Is there to be any adjudication in this case?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend
is a lawyer; I have mentioned the names of the distinguished jurists who are to act as members of this commission.

To gather the evidence;
but is there to be any adjudication?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If I understand
the word adjudication, it is making a finding upon evidence. To show the absolute fairness of the Government and its desiTe to 1 obtain the truth and establish the facts, the Prime Minister has offered to my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition the privilege of appointing a Counsel before the commission.

That is to gather the
evidence,- but will this commission make any decision?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend,
as I say, is a lawyer, and I have read the scope of the commission. The commission is to adjudicate upon the evidence; to make its finding upon the evidence before it. As I have stated, a Royal Commission can have no other purpose and object than the
ascertainment of the facts. On the other hand, members of a committee of the House, especially on a party question, are bound to be actuated more or less by political considerations. There is also some aiming at political effect, and above all, there is delay, which may be of the greatest injustice to the parties whose honour may be concerned. I would call the attention of the hon. member for Wright to the following words which I quote from the Order in Council appointing the commission:
Also to inquire into such other matters relating to the acts or proceedings of the Shell Committee as may be referred to the said comissioners by Order in Council from time to time, and to report the result of any such further inquiries with the evidence taken therein.
The Commission is to investigate and of course to report. There, is precedent, I think, in the case of all Governments for the appointment of Royal Commissions, but I desire to call the attention of my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition to the course of procedure which has been followed by Government representing the Liberal party; I shall refer only to these. In Saskatchewan at the present time three Royal Commissions are engaged in investigating charges against members of the Administration and members of the House. In Manitoba the Morris Government, I am told, has appointed two Royal Commissions. Sir Oliver Mowat was looked upon as one of the foremost statesmen of Ontario, and, later, in Dominion politics. In 1884, he gave a Royal Commission to investigate an alleged attempt to corrupt certain members of the Legislature. The late Sir George Ross, at that time Hon. G. W. Ross, Premier of Ontario, appointed two judges-Mr. Chancellor Boyd, if my memory serves me correctly, and Mr. Justice Falconbridge-to investigate the so-called Gainey charges. I desire to read the remarks which were made by Hon. G. W. Ross in connection with appointment of that commission. He expressed his preference for this method over that of a committee of the Legislature. He said:
The Commitee of Privileges and Elections is necessarily a committee composed of a majority of supporters of the Government and any special committee that would be given would be similarly composed. The investigation, of course, would be open. The committee have the power to swear witnesses, send for persons papers and so forth. They have large powers, but not larger powers than the statute enables us to give a commission. No matter what their finding be, if they exculpated the Provincial Secretary it would be said to be a partisan finding. A royal commission was better, in his
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen recall the investigation? During the session of 1899, on motion of Mr. Borden, an investigation was opened by the Committee on Privileges and Elections into the West Huron and Brockville elections. The result was that only the West Huron election was looked into by Parliament, and that only in a partial manner; it was dragged along as one would expect. When Mr. Borden moved for a scrutiny again in 1900, the Government, under the leadership of the right hon. leader of the Opposition, changed its mind and refused to send the question to the Committee on Privileges and Elections. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, speaking on the motion of Mr. Borden, said in part (Hansard, 1900, page 5672):
If I understand aright the language of the hon. member for York, N.B. (Mr. Foster), he is disposed to agree with us in this that there should be an inquiry full and complete.
Not partial-(full and complete.	[DOT]
Hear, hear-not. partial.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not partial. Now, let us see how my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition was going to get a full inquiry:
Taking West Huron if need be, taking Brockville if need be, taking every other place in which these offences have been committed. If we agree on this it is settled ; the Government is ready to do its part. Now, a tribunal must

do this work. What shall it be? Do you think that this work can be adequately performed by the Committee of Privileges and Elections? No one believes that. Do you think that this work can be adequately performed by any committee of'this House? Nobody believes that.
This is a Daniel come to judgment.
A belated Daniel.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Nobody believes that. What body other than a tribunal-
Not a committee.
-or a court should do that? It must be a judicial court, a judicial inquiry of the fullest character, and this is the policy which I have to offer to friends of the Government and to opponents of the Government as well.
Which he never carried out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Which he never carried out? That only goes to show how little I knew about my right hon. friend and the course which he followed with regard to matters of this kind. Here he states that this is the way and the only way. Now he says this is not the way, and I am told that when he said this was the way and the only way, he did not adopt that way. Well, my right hon. friend has an interesting personality. Custom cannot stale his infinite variety. But I think he will have some difficulty in making to this House and this country an excuse and a justification for his refusal to accept this Royal Commission, composed of the Chief Justices of Ontario, and one of the most eminent of the justices of the Supreme Court of Canada, clothed with complete power to investigate and report upon the matter at issue, with the privilege or the opportunity afforded to him of naming his own counsel, so that his party may be represented and anything they desire to be laid before the tribunal may be laid before them and there judicially and impartially considered.
So much for the precedents for the employment of a judicial committee to investigate charges or suggestions such as have been put forward by my hon. friend from Richmond. As I have said, my right hon. friend will have some difficulty in convincing this House and the country that he had good reason to adopt the attitude that the proposal of the right hon. the Prime Minister was unacceptable. The only alternative is that my right hon. friend for some reason objects to the personnel of the commission. As to that, he will be able to state his views if he so desires ; but certainly, in the minds of the people of this country, no more capable, no more eminent, no more trustworthy judges could1 be selected by this Government for the purpose of making an inquiry regarding these contracts, sifting the evidence, establishing the facts, and rendering the true finding. I hesitate to say that my right hon. friend is actuated in any way by a desire to make political capital at this time out of charges or suggestions made respecting the administration by this Shell Committee. But if my right hon. friend did so desire, and if he followed the course which has been adopted recently by his party in sending out tons of literature containing erroneous and misleading statements, insinuations, rumours, hearsays, I should imagine that he would obtain a fair amount of additional ammunition by an inquiry before a committee of this House, in which the laws of evidence would be entiiely disregarded, and in which, as I have stated, assertion would take the place of fact. I believe that the House and the country have been surprised at the attitude of the right hon. leader of the Opposition with regard to the announcement of the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister has met the -I will not say charges-the suggestions, the insinuations of the hon. member for Richmond, and he has met them promptly, he has met them decisively, and he has met them in such a way as has appealed to the judgment of the people of this country.
So far as concerns the remarks of the hon. member for Richmond, with respect to these fuse contracts, and the other allegations which he has made respecting profits or commissions, I do not propose to say anything further. I have dealt with them only as showing the ground upon which the Government has acted in the appointment of a Royal Commission to investigate all the facts. I have stated that the hon. member for Richmond, in making the suggestions or insinuations which he did, introduced a new element into the debate. Neither the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), nor the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell), nor the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), nor the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte), until he touched upon the question of these contracts, made any charges or insinuations against the honour or integrity of any member of this House or any member of the Shell Committee.
Resuming the argument upon the motion of my right hon. friend the leader of the

Opposition, upon the question as to whether or not a general inquiry, shall be held by a committee of this House upon the administration of the Shell Committee, the position of the Government is as has been indicated by the right hon, the leader of the Government and by the speakers who followed him on this side. Let me repeat, the Shell Committee was not an agent of the Dominion Government. The Shell Committee was not, as has been stated, a branch of any department of the Dominion Government.

Does my hon. friend
say that it was a trustee of the Imperial Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Shell Committee was an agent of the Imperial Government, not of the Government of Canada. The Canadian Pacific railway, I believe, has been an agent of the Imperial Government in the purchase of supplies in Canada. Would it be a proper course for this Government, apart from a request on the part of the Imperial Government, to investigate the purchases made by the Canadian Pacific railway for the Imperial Government? The Hudson Bay Company is, I believe, an agent for the French Government. Would it be proper for this Government, apart from a request by the French Government, to investigate the purchases made by the Hudson Bay Company for the French Government, and paid for by money provided by the French Government? Let me repeat, Mr. Speaker, that not one cent of the public moneys of the Dominion of Canada has been expended by the Shell Committee. The Dominion Government has paid no accounts of the Shell Committee. The Shell Committee has never been in privity with the Dominion Government. The Shell Committee was named by the Minister of Militia and, as the Prime Minister has stated, the Government Of Canada is' responsible for the character of the men, or at least for its action in naming, through the Minister of Militia, the personnel of the Shell Committee.
Is a trust fund not as sacred as an ordinary fund?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend has missed the point. Trust funds are more sacred than ordinary funds. An agency is a form of trust, but the agency in this case was an agency of the Imperial Government, and the trust in this case was a trust for the Imperial Government.

Let me summarize again. The Shell Committee was the agent of the Imperial Government, taking its instructions from the Imperial Government, reporting to the Imperial Government, and spending the money of the Imperial Government. The Shell Committee did not act for the Dominion Government; it took no step on the authorization of the Dominion Government. The Dominion Government bad no authority to interfere in any manner, shape or form with the discretion exercised by the Shell Committee,, and where there is ho authority, I contend that there can be no responsibility. If the Government had had authority to say to the Shell Committee, you must place this order here, and you must place that order there; you must not pay more than a certain price for this article, or more than a certain price for that article; you must buy at this price, or not at all, then the Shell Committee would have been the agent of this Government, but that was precisely not the case. The Shell Committee derived no authority from this Government; the Shell Committee did not act under instructions from this Government; the Shell Committee paid out none of the moneys of this country. I am aware that my hon. friend from St. John, in lawyer fashion-he always introduced the subtlety of the lawyer into his speeches in this House-
The minister himself is a lawyer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I was reduced. My hon. friend from St. John says: "Oh, 'but is Canada not going to pay her full share in this war." Undoubtedly, and I regret very much that in 1899 Canada did not pay her full share of the war; it is a pity that we did not. Canada is going to pay her full share of the war, and Canada is paying to-day all the accounts that can be paid by Canada to-day. But with regard to the men at the front, with regard to the munitions they use on the firing line, with regard to the equipment which they may require, and with regard to the hospital and transportation services, it is perfectly obvious that Canada is not in a position to pay because the accounts can not yet be adjusted. To carry my hon. friend's argument to its logical conclusion, this would be the result: If the Shell Committee here is spending the public moneys of Canada, by reason of the fact that Canada will ultimately pay a share of the cost of munitions used by the British troops in France, and if Parliament, therefore, is entitled to inquire into the expenditures of the Shell Committee, then it must follow that the public moneys of Canada are toeing expended by the Imperial Government in purchasing in the United States and in the United Kingdom. speechtext:

The further question arises, as I stated in the earlier portion of my remarks on Tuesday last With regard to making public at this time confidential communications passing between the War Office and the Shell Committee relating to orders for shells, to difficulties of financing, etc. Personally I can hardly conceive that the British Government would toe willing that confidential communications, letters and telegrams disclosing the urgency of their needs, the shells which they intend to use, and their other requirements'-information which would, in a sense, disclose their future strategy in the field-I can hardly conceive that the British Government would be willing to have that information made public by .an inquiry such as my right hon. friend suggests in his motion.

They can investigate fuses, but not shells.
.Sir THOMAS WHITE: My right hon. friend is still unwilling to make the distinction I made some time ago. A suggestion involving the standing of a minister is one thing, and an investigation into the ordinary administration of the Shell Committee is another, and a very different thing. What position did my right hon. friend take when an inquiry was asked for at the time of the Boer War, when the Department of Agriculture, not an outside committee, was engaged as agent toy the British Government to purchase hay and oats? Did my right hon. friend consent to an investigation into the purchases and

expenditures made by the Department of Agriculture on behalf of the British Government? No. He took the ground that no such investigation should be held, contending that while it was competent for Parliament to investigate the expenditure of the public money of Canada, it was not competent for Parliament to investigate the expenditure of money of the Imperial Parliament. That was the position he took in 1903, when the war h^d been, over for a year. There was then no question of disclosing information which might 'be of advantage to the enemy, yet my right hon. friend squarely took the position that although the Department of Agriculture had purchased for the Imperial Government, and had spent the money of the Imperial Government, no investigation should be held because it was not the money of Canada that had been spent. In the face of the position he took then, how can he demand, while the war is raging, an investigation into the administration of the Shell Committee, involving as it does the disclosure of all confidential communications passing between the War Office and its agent, the Shell Committee. That will be for him to explain. It is true that in the midst of the Crimean War there was an investigation, and how did it result? It resulted precisely as was foreseen by statesmen of that time, The inquiry was wholly abortive and wholly without result. For reasons of state, evidence could not 'be produced, and when the committee finally made its report it was absolutely valueless. The case is different when the honour of a member of the Government is at issue. If a charge, an accusation, or an insinuation is made with respect to the conduct of a member of this Government, it is for this Government to protect its honour by ordering an, investigation, whether it touches the transactions of the Shell Committee, or .any other transactions taking place in Canada, or by parties in Canada. The Government, has nothing to hide, nothing to conceal. We desire that the facts shall be established. We desire that the truth shall prevail. We have appointed a tribunal in which the people of this country have implicit confidence, and we have empowered that tribunal to inquire into every fact and circumstance touching the transactions in which the hon. member for Richmond sought to connect Col. Allison and his commissions with the Minister of Militia. I say that for the administration of the Shell 
Committee we are not responsible. But the Government would be responsible if it allowed suggestions, accusations, or charges to he made against a minister without taking effectual steps to enable them to be either proved or disproved.
I have dealt at greater length than I intended with the speech of my hon. friend from Richmond, in which he made the accusations to which I have referred, and I have dealt in a- general way with the motion moved by my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition for an inquiry. I have stated the position of the Government with regard to the ordinary business transactions of the Shell Committee. Our position is that they are not our agents; we have no authority over them whatsoever, as we have no authority whatsoever over the Imperial Munitions Board; and having no authority over the Shell Committee, there cannot be on the part of this Government any responsibility for its action,. The Prime Minister has stated that as the Shell Committee is the agent of the Imperial Governr ment, he will direct the attention of that Government to every statement made in this House against their administration, and it will then be for the Imperial Government to say whether it desires an investigation into the administration of its agent, the Shell Committee-an investigation into the prices at which it authorized the Shell Committee to purchase shells, and into the question of the distribution of orders. But that is a question for the Imperial Government and not for this Government. If in the course of this debate a charge, an accusation, an insinuation or a suggestion, is made which by implication would appear to involve the conduct of a minister, the Prime Minister has taken the position tnat in such a case the Government will say: We have constituted a tribunal of eminent jurists, and we shall refer the whole matter to them; we will give them authority to inquire into all the facts, and will ask them to make an impartial, an unfair-an impartial,' a fair and unbiassed finding.	,

Mr. Speaker, the House has listened with a great deal of patience to the address delivered by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White). On such an occasion as this, when speaking for the Government for the first time, after grave accusations involving the administration of the public affairs of this country have been presented to the House, my hon. friend, I am quite satisfied, has not made such a deliverance as the House and the country have looked for. Satisfied as my hon. friend usually is with his discussions of public questions, I am sure that he is not satisfied with himself to-day, and I am quite sure that the House and the country will not be satisfied with his statement nor with the position which he has taken. One cannot summarize my hon. friend's position better than by stating, first, that he declared that there was nothing to investigate; secondly, that he argued that it was impossible to investigate; and, thirdly, that he announced that the Government were going to investigate. That is my hon. friend's case put in a nutshell. By declaring and reiterating time after time, in the course of his laboured utterance, that the Government are not responsible for the Shell Committee, he leaves the House and the country to infer the fact, that the Government are not xe-sponsible for J. W. Allison and his doings. J. W. Allison was part of the Shell Committee; he was the direct agent of this Government and of the Shell iCommitttee in negotiating the contracts fox fuses in the United (States. My hon. friend cannot evade the responsibility for the position taken by iCol. J. Wesley Allison. I am reminded by my ho.n. friend's position to-day of a little remark which he made when he closed the debate on Tuesday night. He told us that my hon. friend from Carle-ton (Mr. Carvell) had sent out an S.O.S. call to the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte). If he did he received a splendid
response. Well, my hon. friend has been sending out S.O.S. calls to all parts of the country, and the responses which he has been receiving have not been in the way of assistance or approval of the course which he and the Government have taken in regard to this matter.
My hon. friend on Tuesday night, in a laboured argument, declared that there was nothing to investigate, that this Government should not investigate, that the Imperial Government and its interests were paramount, and that this Government could not move in the matter. His leader, the Prime Minister, within forty-eight hours, absolutely swept away all those petty arguments by proceeding to appoint a commission without consulting the Imperial Government in the matter at all. If the Prime Minister can, in regard to one phase of this subject, appoint a commission to investigate certain facts, the argument is absolutely indisputable that he has the same right and power to provide for an investigation such as is asked for by the leader of the Opposition in regard, to every phase of the subject. My hon. friend says: "We are not responsible for the Shell Commission." It is true that they appointed the Shell Committee, that they selected the members out of all the eligible men in the Dominion, and that they committed to them the task of finding shells in Canada to sell to the British Government. We have heard many statements as to the Shell Committee submitting all its contracts to the Imperial authorities. I do not know whether my hon. friend has made any investigation into that question; but, if he had, he would have found that what was done by the Shell Committee was this: that they entered into a solemn contract with the Imperial Government by which they became, not the agents of the Imperial Government, but the agents appointed by this Government of the Dominion of Canada, and contractors with the Imperial Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does my hon. friend mean to say that they became the agents of this Government in a contract?

My hon. friend and his Government selected the members of the Shell Committee and appointed them a body to deal with this question of providing shells and other munitions to aid in the war. This Government became responsible for them and they were its representatives and creation.
(Some hon. MEMBERS: No.

And as its representatives they entered into a contract with the Imperial Government. My hon. friend will not deny that there is on .record a contract with the Imperial Government signed by every member of the old Shell Committee, by which they contracted to make and deliver certain shells at certain prices-that they were not the agents, in any .sense of the word, of the Imperial Government, but contractors with them. Yet my hon. friend disclaims responsibility for the members of the Shell Committee. He told us the other night, in regard to the allegations which were made and which he was unable to. controvert, that the Shell Committee had made mistakes. If they have made mistakes, why should my hon. friend not grant the committee moved for by the right hon. leader of the Opposition in order to find out what the mistakes are and how in the interest of the country they can be corrected in the future?
My hon. friend admits that the fuse contracts entered into by Allison should he a matter of investigation. Why should it not be equally a matter of investigation to find out how the other parts of the shells were made and the contracts in regard to them entered into? My hon. friend cannot logically differentiate between the propriety of investigating into contracts to make fuses, which are an essential part of a shell, and the propriety of investigating into contracts to make the steel part of a shell or to provide the boxes into which the shells are put after the fuses are attached; but that is what my hon. friend endeavours to do. The people, of this country will not permit such a fine distinction to be drawn in regard to this question. They realize that the whole question has reached such a stage that it should be investigated, and we hear from all parts of Canada in tones of thunder the demand that the whole question should be investigated to the fullest possible extent.
My hon. friend the other night, while he was lumbering along in very deep water, finding the going very hard, digressed for a moment to chastise my hon. friend from Richmond because he referred to a contract made by the Minister of Militia with J. W. Allison for Colts revolvers and pistols. My hon. friend has referred to perjury before the Davidson Commission. I think it might be well to await the report of that commission.

But if my hon. friend is too impatient to await that report, I think he owes it to himself and to this House, if he desires prosecution, to lay an information against the party complained of.

Q. What orders were given for automatic pistols?-A. The first order is one for 1,000 automatic pistols given on the 5th September to Col. J. W. Allison, by authority of an Order in Council pf that date. I have the Order in Council here before me.
The Minister of Finance took the point that J. Wesley Allison's name was not mentioned in the Order in Council. Did not they know this man who, according to the colleague of these hon. gentlemen, 'as declared .in tins House only one short month ago, had saved to the people of Great Britain and Canada no less than fifty million dollars. Do hon. gentlemen opposite mean to tell us that the men who have been directing the

affairs of the department since the 4th of August, 1914, when the department was spending these tremendous sums of money, did not know J. Wesley Allison and all about him? It is all very well for the Minister of Finance to say that he does not know John Wesley Allison. A nice guardian of the treasury he is. With contracts involving millions upon millions of dollars upon which, according to his own colleague, this man had saved fifty million dollars, this Minister of Finance says that he does not know the gentleman who is effecting these tremendous economies. I am asking you.

I may say further concerning Col. Allison

-" I want it distinctly understood that I do not want any profit added to the price under any conditions, with the intention of providing a commission for me, as I would not under any circumstances accept a commission of any kind from anybody, in connection with this matter.

ada were thrown open in order that these goods might be brought in? speechtext:

that my hon. friend is not in a position to dispute the truth of the arguments of the hon. member for Richmond. But my hon. friend did produce a guarantee from a viery well known trust company in New York, and the information was given that the effect of this guarantee was that the Shell Committee and the country would get back the money in the event of the contract being cancelled. I should like to call my hon. friend's attention to one peculiar clause in this contract, which shows that this guarantee may or may not be worth very much. After providing for the condition that shall exist if the company is in arrears, this clause is inserted:
But the company shall not be held responsible otherwise for the non-performance of this agreement due to any cause beyond Its reasonable control.	,
* The result of that is that this agreement, which my hon. friend produces, does not guarantee in any way to the Shell Committee, or to the Government interested, the payment of any damages in the event of the company failing to perform its contract. The gentlemen who negotiated this contract on behalf of the Shell Committee were General Bertram and Mr. David Carnegie, in conjunction with Colonel Allison. Colonel Allison was acting both ways; he was acting for the Shell Committee, and he was acting with Mr. Yoakum, his side partner. Allison and Yoakum made an agreement with the Shell Committee by which they were to supply 2,500,000 fuses at an average price of $4.25, the total value of that contract being $10,416,667, and they were to receive an advance of ten per cent immediately, or $1,141,000. They weire to receive one-half of that amount, some $525,000 odd, within four months after that date. The effect of the arrangements that were made in regard to the matter, was that the Shell Committee went into partnership with Allison and Yoakum and those two munition companies, and .agreed to find them the money with which to begin business, advancing to each of them, according to the proportion of the amount of the contract they held, a sum of money, in the case of the American- Ammunition Company amounting to $1,400,000 to begin with, and half a million more after three months. They -said: "You go out and make the fuses and we will always provide $1,000,000 for you in the treasury; if by any possibility you fall down, there will be no action of damages against you, we will not try to recover anything from you for breach of con-
tract in any way; our only recourse is that, according to the method worked out in clauses 13 and 15 of this contract, a certain proportion of this advance must come back to us." Is that a wise or a businesslike proposition? And here we have the evidence as to the result of the proposition in the agreement which was made between Yoabum and Bassick and Cadwell, wherein it is recited1 that:
Whereas, the said K. B. Cadwell and Company Incorporated, and said Yoakum, and said Bassick, are together entitled to receive as their total and aggregate commission for negotiating and effecting said contract the sum of $1,000,000 in- the whole, being at the rate of 40 cents per fuse.
The result, putting it in a comprehensive form, was that this Shell Committee went down, to New York; they found these irres-ponsibles whom nobody knows anything about; they made this contract of partnership with them by which they were .able to make a profit of 40 cents upon every one of the two and a half, million fuses included in the contract; and they proceeded to divide the spoils. Colonel Bertram and Mr. Carnegie were in New York at that time, and the minister himself tells us all about that. We are not left to .any conjecture in regard to that matter. The Minister of Militia tells us what went on about fuses, how this contract was let:
I come to the question of fuses, and I doubt not that what I have to say on that subject will be startling to some hon. gentlemen. I do not wish to indulge in personal criticism, or to say anything to make any hon. gentlemen opposite feel aggrieved; but I have here the facts and figures, and I challenge the freest and fullest inquiry into them all.
The hon. gentlemen heard that. The minister's colleagues sat around him and heard him say that. He went on to tell us how he had made the contract:
Imagine our surprise when Col. Bertram told me that they were asking $6 apiece for these fuses. I sent for Col. Allison and said to him that this price was absurd, that we should get them for easily half that, and so fire two shots instead of one at these gentlemen who are seeking to overthrow the liberties of the British Empire and of the French nation. Col. Allison brought the price down to $5.10; later, to $4.90, which is the lowest price for which I have heard of any company in the United States, the Morgans or any other, making fuses for the British Government. Later Col. Allison brought the price down to $4.50, and, by still further organization to $4.25. Contracts were made at this price of $4.25 for these time fuses. But, owing at least in part to the fact that a number of firms in the United States had been blown up, and there was more or less of the "German peril " idea abroad, they refused to take tile contract, and it remained at $4.50.: Thus there

was a saving of 40 cents on each fuse, or a total saving to the British Government of $1,600,000 in that one deal alone.
Then my hon. friend went on to say that
A contract was let in the United States at $4 -and I may say that Colonel Allison never heard of that contract until it had been let.
I wonder what happened that the colonel did not know about it. That was something strange.
Subsequently, a month later, a contract was let at $3.50, with the price of $4 to a firm in Canada, who, I believe got their fuses largely made in the United States.
I will deal with the question of the Canadian contract a little later on. But I want to call the attention of the House and the country to this fact, that standing in his place in Parliament, in the presence of his colleagues, the Minister of Militia, knowing that they knew that Col. Allison was his guide, philosopher, and friend, and had been since August, 1914, told this story -of this fuse contract on account of which hon. gentlemen to-day are appointing a commission of investigation. Hon. gentlemen cannot saddle the responsibility of this question upon General Hughes alone. Each and every one of them, from the Prime Minister down, stands with General Hughes on account of these facts, responsible for everything that has been done in regard to these fuse contracts in the United States.
Let me give another fact. I am informed on reliable information from gentlemen oi standing who I believe will substantiate this statement before a proper tribunal, that at the time General Bertram and Carnegie were in the United States a responsible person came to them and offered to com struct and deliver the fuses which were dedesired by them upon the basis of being paid for their cost of production, plus 5 per cent. While this matter was under consideration, John Wesley Allison arrived. So this gentleman asked him to add 75 cents to the price of each fuse for the purpose of dividing that amount of money into four different parts, of which one was to be kept by the contractor, he was to have one, and the others were to be given to parties unknown. General Bertram and Mr. Carnegie declined to do business with this man, who was willing to deliver those fuses for their cost price, plus 5 per cent; and they proceeded to make this contract with Yoakum, Cadwell and this crowd of speculators who are trafficking with Canadian money, and, as my right hon. leader pointed out, on account of their failure to perform that contract, have been trafficking in the lives of our boys who nave been fighting for this Empire on the other side of the Atlantic.
This contract was made with those people on June 19. On May 26, 1915, a responsible Canadian organization offered in writing to make delivery of fuses to the Shell Committee for $4.20 per fuse. Mark you, Mr. Speaker, that was on May 26. On July 25, the Shell Committee, after they had made the arrangement with the United States people, offered to these Canadians an order for
250.000	fuses at $4 each, and an order for
250.000	at $3, or a net price of $3.50 per fuse, or 75 cents per fuse less than the price at which contracts had been let to the companies in the United States. That is very significant, Mr. 'Speaker, in view of Allison's position in regard to the amount that was to be divided. Nothing was done by the Shell Committee until August 17, when a contract was made with the Canadians. When the contract was made, on August 17, the Canadian gentlemen asked Mr. Carnegie whether or not he would give them an advance to assist them in carrying out their contract. Mr. Carnegie said: no, that the Shell Commitee had never made advances. Later on, these Canadian gentlemen, having ascertained about the contracts in the United States, asked in a letter that they be allowed 15 per cent by way of an advance.
Who were those men?

If a committee oi this House is granted my hon. friend will get the names. The money was not advanced to these Canadian gentlemen as it was advanced,to the people in the United States; it was deposited in a bank in Toronto, under certain limited conditions. I have given the situation on May .26, before this contract was entered into in the United States. Responsible Canadians offered to make shells at a price less than that at which the Shell Committee gave the contract in the United States. Why was this? The Minister of Militia told us of the wonderful performances- of John Wesley Allison; of how this and that was arranged; and of how different contracts had been made at prices from $6 to $4.25. But before the prices were driven down, here were Canadian gentlemen willing and able to enter into a contract, and they were disregarded. On what principle was that done? The Government is responsible, because the Minister of Militia knew all about it. This Minister of Militia is not a Dr. Jekyll and

a Mr. Hyde. He is not a minister one day when he sits in 'Council, and some other kind of person when not in Council. Collective responsibility on the part of a Government for the actions of its individual members has not yet departed under the constitutional practices of this country. That has been well settled by many known precedents, and our constitution has been built up on precedent upon precedent. No Government can say we do not know of the actions of a colleague when there is evidence which shows that they must have known if they had exercised ordinary common sense and prudence in regard to such an important matter as the tremendous expenditures which have been made by this country in connection with the war.
In Canada we have a responsible company which on March 5, 1916, shipped 50,000 fuses, which, from March 5 to March 31. shipped1 100,000, amd which delivered 25,000 more than they had agreed to do in their contract. On April 6 they will ship 25,000 more, and they are in a position to make
30,000	fuses per week. If this Government, or the Shell Committee, had made the slightest effort, or had been animated by any desire to secure the making of these fuses in Canada, they could have made the contract with Canadians on May 26 instead of becoming involved in disgraceful arrangements with a group of speculators in the city of New York. My hon. friend the Minister of Militia said with regard to these matters, that the Government have constituted a tribunal, and that nobody must say anything about it.. It is true, he said that the Shell Committee had made mistakes, and he went on to make the surprising statement that if the Shell Committee had placed the orders with Canadian manufacturers, they would not have been responsible if there had been delay. In the case under consideration, they declined to place the orders with Canadian manufacturers, and they deliberately placed them with American manufacturers, and they are responsible for the delay. This Government permitted them to place those orders, and the Government are responsible for the delay. If the Shell Committee made mistakes, as the Government admits, on what possible ground, without traversing the facts that have been placed before the House, can hon. gentlemen opposite refuse an investigation wide enough to take within its purview the actions of the Shell Commit-

tee which have been complained of not merely by the press supporting hon. gentlemen on this side, but as my hon. friends opposite know, by some of the leading journals supporting them. These journals have demanded an investigation of the widest character.
My hon. friend the Minister of Finance asks what purpose there would toe in holding an investigation. He was something like my hon. friend from Calgary who will now imagine I presume, that he is inspired by some holy fire and has a divine right to be a prophet when he recalls that a few weeks ago he predicted that when the war was over some reputations would suffer. He told the House of the awful catastrophe that he was sure was going to happen after the war was over and of the reputations that were to be shattered, but he wanted to postpone the evil day. My hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) has well pointed out the evil of delay in regard to such matters. Records will toe lost, and where will the men who constitute t'he brood of speculators in New York toe when the war is over? Where will the men who have been trafficking in the people's money toe then? Will they toe within the jurisdiction of this House, or of this country, when the war is over? My hon. friend from Richmond made that point very effectively, and there is no answer to it. Yet, the Minister of Finance' asks: What purpose is to be served in holding an investigation, and have we a right to investigate without the Imperial Government's consent. Yes, we have a right, because the Prime Minister has proceeded to investigate. He did not ask the Colonial Secretary or the War Office whether he would issue this commission. He read the other day the correspondence he had had with the home authorities. Was there anything to indicate that he had asked for permission to issue this commission. On the contrary, he announced the commission, and sent word to Sir George Perley to intimate to the Colonial Office that he had issued a commission. So the arguments of the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) of my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett); and of the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White), go for nought in face of the fact that without asking permission, and absolutely on its own authority, for the good government of Canada, and in the interests of the public business of this country, the Government has issued a commission.

The question is, will this Commission cover the case? I venture to say that hon. gentlemen who are familiar with the doings of the Davidson Commission will not think that this Royal Commission is of a character that will satisfy the country. What is the situation? Under the Act which provides for public inquiries, we appoint two eminent judges. These two judges have powers in so far as the investigation is concerned, only to the extent to which this Parliament gives them power. The history of investigations into public matters shows that Parliament, composed as it is of the representatives of a free people, has reserved to itself the right to investigate matters of public business. Why have we a Public Accounts Committee empowered to summon witnesses and take evidence, unless it is for the purpose of enabling the representatives of the people through that committee to investigate to the fullest extent, if they desire, the expenditures that have been made on Consolidated Account, but, apparently, according to hon. gentlemen opposite, we should get some outside body to make that investigation year after year.
This Royal Commission is appointed under the Inquiries Act. I see by the American papers that J. Wesley Allison is at Seabreeze in Florida. Let us suppose that the commission sent an officer down there to serve Col. Allison with a subpoena. In the first place, the writ would not run beyond the confines of Canada. Col. Allison need not pay the slightest attention to a writ of that kind; and he would not come. The best evidence that he would not come is the fact that he has not already come. He has been in contempt of the Parliament of Canada since February last. This Government knew, when it appointed this commission, that it would have no authority whatever for getting hold of Allison or Yoakum or any other of the men who were concerned in these shell transactions in New York or some other part of the United States. Hon. gentlemen opposite knew that this commission from its very inception will be absolutely nugatory. It will no more get Allison or Yoakum before it than the Davidson Commission could get Keever. Its powers in that particular are absolutely nugatory. If this Government was in earnest in regard to the appointment of a tribunal of a judicial character, they would not be satisfied with appointing a commission merely with the bald powers given in the Inquiries Act, but would introduce and pass a measure constituting a
court with the widest possible powers that a federal court can have. I challenge the Minister of Justice to say that any writ issued by this commission under the Inquiries Act will be of the slightest value beyond the boundary of Canada. He knows very well that it will not. He knows that legislation could be introduced constituting a court on broader lines and with wider powers-a court that would be respected by the comity of nations, where one nation assists another in enforcing the law. I say, therefore, that the investigation proposed by the Government is of no value and of no effect, and they know it. Do hon. gentlemen realize how grave a matter this is? ' The people of this country, in this the moment of her peril, are not pardoning, and will not pardon, the men who traffic in munitions of war at the cost of the lives of our sons who have gone to fight the battles of the Empire. This Parliament would be justified in sitting continuously and exercising through a special committee the widest possible powers in order to have the fullest investigation into every phase of this matter. A Committee of Parliament such as we ought to have could continue its investigations until Allison and the other men had been brought back and the whole matter cleared up. Why does not the Minister of Justice cause proceedings to be taken against Allison and have him extradited? Hon. gentlemen opposite hope that Parliament will prorogue in a short time, perhaps, before the Minister of Militia gets back from the other side, and that the whole matter will be hung up in the limbo of uncertainty and forgetfulness through the tedious and wearisome proceedings of a commission, whose decrees will not be respected by a single one of the men who ought to be brought before it. They hope that with the forgetfulness that time brings public interest in the matter will wane, and the conscience of Canada go to sleep. That is their theory, and that is why they have appointed this tribunal, which will be absolutely nugatory, and which is known to foe so by every lawyer in the country. Hon. gentlemen can not escape responsibility by declaring, as the Minister of Finance did this afternoon, that they do not know this man Allison. The Minister of Finance said that hardly any of his colleagues knew him. What a strange combination of men we have in the Cabinet of this country! Why, the name of Allison has been in everybody's mouth for the last year and a half. Beyond a shadow of doubt.

as I have already pointed out, there must have 'been knowledge of Allison on the part of some members of the Government. When the Minister of Militia told the Minister of Customs that Allison was acting as his agent in the purchase of war supplies in the United States, and was arranging for the free entry of these supplies into Canada, how can any one say that the Minister of Customs did not know anything about Allison? He knew, before he permitted the goods to come in, that he was employed by the Minister of Militia. The very statement of the proposition is evidence of the fact. Other members of the Cabinet must 'have known about him too. The Minister of Militia is no more responsible for J. Wesley Allison than any other man who sits in the Cabinet, and the country ought to know it. The occasion is one that demands drastic action by the Government. The hon. member for Dundas (Mr. Broder), if he is correctly reported, said:
I am getting too near the end of my life to be expected to object to holding an investigation into the work of the Shell Committee. I went to the Premier and told him that if investigation were decided against I would have to vote against him. He said that if I voted against him it would do him more harm than if almost any other member of the party did so. I replied that I could not alter my view at my time of life, that I would have to go straight to the end. I would have to vote for an inquiry. I don't believe the Premier quite realizes what is going on. These are not the days of the Marlborough wars. The people of Canada are on trial for their honesty. I told the Premier it was no use suggesting to the Imperial Government that they should ask for an investigation. They can't ask the Canadian Government for an investigation. We are the people to deal with this.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The hon. member for Dundas has written me a letter stating that he gave no such interview.

It would be interesting to know just what the hon. member for Dundas did say. He certainly said something; the House and the country know that. We all have the greatest respect for him, and we all know that he will not deny that he said he had no confidence in Allison when he was employed as the agent of this Government in the purchase of war supplies. Why is it that papers that are strong supporters of hon. gentlemen opposite discuss in the frankest way the seriousness of the situation? Here is one which says:	.
Manufacturers who have been Conservatives all their lives are so stricken by the reign of

terror established under the auspices of Sir Robert Borden that they dare not come out in the open and proclaim the truth that ought to be proclaimed in the interests of Canadian industry and Britain's safety. The Shell Committee is the work of Sir Robert Borden's hands. Nobody's head seems to have had any share in the origination of the small piffling Shell Committee, whose waste of money may have been inevitable, and was far less ruinous to the British taxpayer than its waste of time was to the Canadian manufacturer.
It goes on to say that my right hon. friend should grant the fullest and most complete investigation. Hon. gentlemen opposite know that that is the situation in which they stand before this country and before their friends. Therefore, Sir, when they say, in the apologetic and halting manner of the Minister of Finance this afternoon, first, that there is nothing to investigate, and, second, that they have no power to investigate, and then when they endeavour to justify the appointment of a body which, as every hon. member knows, will have no power whatever to reach those men who are across the border in the United States, I say that the Government are not proposing a solution with which this country will be satisfied. It is therefore the duty of this House to support the motion of my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition. Let us, as the representatives of a free people in this Parliament, decide to have a committee appointed- to make the widest kind of investigation in .accordance with the resolution proposed by my right hon. friend. Let us asik the assistance of the Minister of Justice to 'bring here the men that can be brought here. Let this Parliament sit until this wrong is uprooted and until all this scandal is laid bare before the Canadian people; and in that way we shall show to the whole Empire that we Canadians will not accept responsibility for such doings by John Wesley Allison and others, as have been exposed, and that we want those high standards of public life, for which our boys are fighting in the old land, which will not permit the continuance of such doings as have been exposed before the Canadian people.

If no one else wishes to take part in the debate, I would ask that you call it six o'clock.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.
Bill No. 76, for the relief of Christopher Sinclair.-Mr. Douglas.
Consideration of the proposed motion of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, for the appointment of a special committee to inquire into the purchase of shells, etc., resumed.

With the permission of the House, I would like to speak for a few moments. I do not wish to intervene before the right hon. leader of the Opposition addresses the House, but, as my name has been made a subject of controversy, I think I should say a few words now. I do not seek any great publicity, and I desire to say that I never gave any authority for an interview which has recently appeared in the newspapers, nor did I make any statement to anybody to be made public. While I am on my feet, I wish to state how I intend to vote, for I do not wish to give a silent vote on this occasion. A good deal has been said of the wisdom or unwisdom of investigating the Shell Committee's business. The argument largely used is that the money spent was British money. Now, Sir, I look upon this war as a partnership between Great Britain and her colonies, and I think we are just as much interested in the outlay of British money as in the outlay of our own money. I do not think the people of this country will be satisfied unless they feel assurance that there is to be pretty thorough investigation. I am glad to see the right hon. leader of the Government (Sir Robert Borden) go as far as he has gone; but I wish he would go further. I do not think that anything short of the fullest investigation will satisfy the public feeling of this country to-day. I do not think that grafters should be allowed to hide in the shadow of this great war, to plot against the interest of the country, and to feed on her revenues. I think the people of Canada are alive to the situation; and, while we believe it is not wise to say too much or criticise too much during the war, we have but to look across the water to see that public opinion, which is always acute and sensitive in Great Britain, was so aroused by the public pres- that it became irresistible, and the Premier of England was obliged to. cross the floor of the House and change the personnel of his Government. These are things that the people notice. While I have no fault to find with the fact that judges are to be appointed to make investigation, and while I am satisfied that they are as competent and as thorough, and better judges of evidence than any committee that this House could appoint, yet the people cannot distinguish between these fine technicalities. I have no fault to find with the fact that judges are appointed, and those who have been appointed have such a standing in the country that the people will be satisfied with their work. But I wish to say further, while I am on my feet, that the people of this country, who are working night and day, who are subscribing money to help the army-the willing sacrifice of an earnest people-feel, as I am sure this House feels, that the money for this war should be properly spent. I intend to vote for the motion of the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition.

Mr. Speaker, after the very powerful address which was delivered this afternoon by my hon. friend from Pictou (Mt.
