I was informed tljat the company was engaged part of the year in carrying timber and part of the year in carrying apples td Liverpool from Nova Scotia in competition with vessels that are not subsidized, charging the highest rate of freight. Unless the carrying of the mails is an excuse for giving them

the $20,000, I do not think there is any other.

We paid them
last year $14,500. They made fewer trips.

My hon. friend from Guysborough has never been very sympathetic towards this vote, but I think there is something to be said in favour of the subsidizing of this service. This steamship company provide a regular service. It is quite possible that at some seasons of the year exporters from Nova Scotia may find shipping facilities, but there would be no certainty about it. In the ease of the apple export trad.e, the apple growers and exporters have the certain knowledge that at a definite time there will be sailings from Halifax to the British market, and that same thing applies to a great many other shippers and exporters. There is that advantage in the subsidizing of this service. I appreciate the objection of the hon. member for Guysborough, namely, that this steamship company is engaged in carrying freight merely and is in competition with shipping owned by private individuals. But private individuals, of course, are always at liberty to receive freight at any port in the world, wherever they can get the best terms, and I fear it would be almost necessary to have a regular freight service from some port in Nova Scotia. Therefore I think the vote is .hardly open to quite the strong objection that my hon. friend always makes to it.
Steamship service between Montreal, Quebec and Manchester, England, during the summer season; and between .St. John, Halifax and Manchester during the winter season, $35,000.
What line runs that service?
That is the Manchester line-the Manchester Mariner, the Manchester Shipper, and so on.
Those boats have not been taken?

These boats have been regular.
Winter steamship service between St. John, Dublin and Belfast, $7,500.
This is an old and long-established service.
What line is engaged in it?
This is the Ulster Steamship Company.
A good Irish name.
Carried.
The name appeals to my hOn. friend.
A New Brunswick company or a British company?
A British company.
How is it that some lines are able to run without their vessels being commandeered?

I do not know, except that their vessels may not be of the kind that would be advantageous for the British Government; yet they are vessels of good capacity, from 3,000 to 6,000 tons. I do not remember any of these vessels having been commandeered.

I see a great complaint in the Newfoundland newspapers in regard to the discrimination which it is alleged is shown in England in regard to the taking and commandeering of certain vessels. I am not particularly anxious to see the vessels in this particular service taken away, but we in Nova Scotia recognize that during the coming summer there will be a shortage of at least half a million tons of coal shipments up the St. Lawrence on account of coal-carrying boats having been taken by the British Government; and, of course, that will have its reactionary effect upon the industry. The position taken by Mr. Cocker, the leader of the Opposition in Newfoundland, in his newspaper during the last few days, is one of indignant protest at the way in which the interests of Newfoundland have suffered from this discrimination. I presume the Government are alive to this situation. My hon. friend says that these British boats of 3,000 to 5,000 tons have not been interfered with. It is rather strange that vessels that are essential to the carrying trade of Canada should be taken off.
Sir GEORGiE FOSTER: In the first place, the British Government does the commandeering. The British Government is at the centre of affairs and knows the necessity, as we in Newfoundland and Canada cannot. I have had a great deal to do with this matter during the past year, and I understand the process; and the more I see of the difficulties of the British Government, the more sympathy I have with them in the enormous task that is

put upon them. Not only has the British Government to commandeer vessels from commercial tonnage for the purpose of British Government transport, but upon the British Government comes the main weight of providing commercial transport for the Allies. Hundreds and hundreds of times these questions have come uip and have been very acute. At first you think it is a mighty shame to take a vessel from this route and put people about, it may be for coal, or for flour, or for something else.
The Newfoundlanders claim that it is flour and provisions.

But when you get to the bottom of it, and learn, as I learned, the necessities, you realize that we have to do some sacrificing as well as as others. Maybe during the present year, if the war goes on, we will see more strenuous times as regards Canada, with reference to our tonnage, than we have ever seen, and we may have to do many things perforce which we would not like to do, and which will interfere with certain channels of trade and cause losses. But the war must go on, and the transportation services must be put through, no matter who suffers. That is attended to by a very competent committee on the other side.
Has the minister seen any evidence of discrimination?

No, I do not think so. In several cases, it looked as if there might have been discrimination, but, when we followed them up, it did not appear that there was. We are in close contact with the Admiralty Committee by cable, and we are also in close contact with them through the High Commissioner, who knows our needs and our necessities. He is a business man, and is well acquainted with what we need, and he has been very assiduous in this matter. Constantly in communication with us, he has also been constantly in communication with the Admiralty Committee which makes the requisitions. I think I am not violating any confidence when I say that, in his reports to us, our High Commissioner carries out the idea I have just expressed of the fairness with which the work is carried on, as against any idea of undue discrimination.

I would like to ask the minister if he is taking into consideration the matter of the apple export trade of Nova Scotia, which comes after the month
of September. The hon. minister knows that the export trade is entirely to Great Britain, and I think we have always been accorded sufficient facilities. I understand, however, that at the end
II p.m. of the present year there is a possibility of insufficient tonnage to carry the apple export trade to Great Britain, and, if the apple producers are unable to export, it will be a very serious matter for Nova Scotia, because the western portion of Nova Scotia is very vitally interested in that particular trade. We are subsidizing, for instance, several lines from the ports of St. John and Halifax to Great Britain, and, giving them a subsidy, we should be in a position to control the char. acter of the traffic which they engage in, if we think that at certain periods of the year we should exercise that power of compelling the steamship owners to discriminate. For instance, if in the month of October it appears desirable that tonnage should be secured for the export of millions of barrels of apples, I submit it would be fair for the Department of Trade and Commerce to insist that the steamers subsidized by that department should disregard other traffic offering at the time and engage exclusively, or almost exclusively, in that particular traffic which is urgent and pressing. I know that in the province of Nova Scotia apple growers are rather apprehensive as to the shipping faciliities for the export of their apples during the present year. I have no particular advice to offer the minister other than that he should take the matter into consideration at an early date and endeavour to make arrangements with the steamship companies which usually engage in this particular trade, and which we subsidize.
If my hon. friend will inquire of the apple producers, he will find that every season I have looked after their interests in every way I possibly could. I have taken a vote of $5,000-

I do not think
that $5,000 has been used for many years; it is not very important.
But it is there for use.
There has been no difficulty as regards tonnage in past seasons, but the difficulty this year will be one of tonnage.

There has been some difficulty in past seasons; there was

last year, but I found that, when the matter was presented to them, the steamship companies were very reasonable in that respect; and, in case after case, I think I was successful in getting apple shipments which at first had not been accepted. But there you are; we will have a certain amount of shipping, and, though the apple industry is important, other industries are also important, and each one presses to have its particular products carried. As far as can reasonably be done, what might be called seasonable freight ought to be looked after, and I think the steamships do. co-operate in that sense.

I did not have an opportunity a minute ago. to say a word on this question of commandeering Canadian vessels. I share with the minister his anxiety as to the necessity of tonnage on the otheT side, and as to the troubles of the British Government. It is our duty to assist them in every way in our power, but I think that our own Government, and not the British Government, should do the commandeering of Canadian ships. I think our own Government should take a stand on this question. We have certain rights in regard to our shipping. We have full control of the trade on the Great Lakes and on the Coast. We make laws in regard to the ships that trade on the inland waters of Canada and on the Coast, independent altogether of the British shipping lines. Our ships .are, of course, British ships, but they carry the Canadian flag. We are, as everybody know's, a nation within a nation, and we have certain rights which we should not abandon to the British Government, even in time of war. My point is that, if Canadian ships are necessary to carry the commerce of the Allies in this war, our own Government should do the commandeering. They could in that way keep track of the situation, and give fair consideration to all the circumstances that surround each case much better than they can do over in London. The Government on the other side do not profess to order us to send soldiers over there to fight the battles of the Empire; they invite us to join them, and we gladly do so. It is all voluntary. Why should our shipping not be on the same basis. I trust I am making myself clear to the minister that he should give the Admiralty to understand that, if they require Canadian tonnage for the purposes of the war, they should apply to the Canadian Government for that tonnage,

and, if we have any to spare, the Canadian Government should do the commandeering itself and hand the tonnage over to the Admiralty for their use. I do not wish to be understood as opposing the commandeering of ships for the war, because we all agree that we must give our last ship as well as our last man and our last dollar in order to win, but I should like the commandeering to come from our Government instead of the British Admiralty.

In the first
place, most of the ships that have been commandeered are British ships, and we should have no authority to commandeer them, whereas the British Government would. In the second place, I think it would be impracticable to carry out the suggestion of my hon. friend, and it would lead to a great deal of trouble at both ends. I think the solution of the matter is rather that the commandeering authorities at London should be in close touch with a representative. of Canada for the purpose of consultation. That is practically being done now through our High Commissioner. I should be very loath to try to understand from my position here the necessities and wants at the centre of the direction of the whole contest. I think it would lead to trouble if I attempted it. However, we are in constant communication with the British authorities, and our views are thoroughly known to them, being represented from, time to time. Hardly a vessel has been commandeered in regard to which there has not been communication between ourselves and the authorities in London.
Winter steam service between St. John, Halifax and London, $15,000.

What line is
that?
Furness, Withy & Co.

Does not the
minister propose to take up vote 158, ocean and mail service between Canada and Great Britain to-night?

As my hon.
friend knows, this service has been very much disorganized. We have not yet concluded arrangement for the coming year, and I did not want to take this vote up until I could give the committee complete information. I expect to conclude the contract before asking the committee to pass the item.

Steam service between Canada and Australia [DOT]or New Zealand or both, on Pacific ocean, $180,50S.

We have had
this contract for a series of years, and it is a very excellent service. The contract ends the middle of this year. The committee might be interested to know that a large quantity of apples are exported to Australia and New Zealand by this service. A very gratifying increase has taken place in that trade. Have we always the
same agents in Australia? I think Mr. Ross represents us there.

Yes, he is a
very excellent agent. Mr. Beddoe represents us in New Zealand.
Steam service between Canada, China and -Japan, $253,333.34.

My hon. friend is no
doubt aware that there was a long debate in the Japanese Diet a few days ago on the question of the treaty between Great Britain and Japan, and reference was also made to the treaty between Japan and Canada. I read a long synopsis of that debate the other day in one of the American papers, and I should like to know if the Government has been approached with regard to a revision of our present treaty with Japan, and whether it has been approached upon the -subject of immigration. The latest available figures show a large increase in Japan

ese immigration to Canada. My hon. friend from British Columbia is very much interested in this question, I know. I may inform him that I receive monthly statements of the Japanese emigration and immigration figures, and these show that about 500 * came to Canada recently. They are classed as returning imigrants, and of course, under the arrangement between the two countries, there is no question about returning immigrants. Are any negotiations taking place between the two countries with regard to immigration, and with regard to the trade treaty? It looks as if there was a strong movement in Japan in favour of a further revision of the treaties, not only between Great Britain and Japan, but between. .Japan and Canada also.
These questions are of course foreign to the subsidy we are discussing.
Are they not ancillary?

The vessels might be ancillary to the immigration, and of course the treaty affects trade between ourselves and Japan. I think I can calm my hon. friend's anxieties as to any present negotiations between the governments. The debate in the Diet was probably like some of the debates we have here-fast and furious there, but not having much effect elsewhere. No negotiations are in progress at present.
What are the last trade figures as between the two countries?

I have not them here, but should be very glad to get them for my hon. friend.
Steam service between Victoria and Saji Francisco, $3,000.

This is an extraordinary
vote:

This is a vote made necessary by 'the terms of Confederation. It was an arrangement which we carried out for many years. I think at first we paid $15,000, and when I was Minister of Finance I took the matter up and found that we were under an obligation to pay a subsidy, but that the amount of the subsidy was not expressly stated. I therefore cut it down to $3,000, but this is a sort of saving grace that is administered, every year.
Will it go on for ever?
For ever and ever as long as British Columbia lasts.

We have settled a great many important matters to-day, and, as it is quite late now and a number of members from the Maritime Provinces who are interested in local services are absent, I would suggest that the committee rise. We will not detain my hon. friend very long on the remaining items.
Was my hon. friend correctly reported the other day when he was reported as having stated in Toronto that it was the intention of the Government to establish what is called a commercial museum?

If my hon. friend will defer that question until I come to my Commercial Estimates I purpose making a little statement to the House.
